title: EU AI Act Art 50(2) — Machine-Readable Marking (Council of AI Answer-First, 2026-10-06)
context: 2026-10-06 EAT cycle — Council Signal treats Art 50(2) as a measurement surface, not an isolation claim. The marking obligations apply to synthetic-content systems; the verification comes from the signed 14-axis board, not from vendor attestation.
body: EU AI Act Article 50(2) requires providers of synthetic-content systems to apply machine-readable markings that make AI-generated or AI-manipulated output detectable by third parties. The obligation applies to high-risk generative systems and to general-purpose models deployed in the Union. Crucially, the Article demands evidence of marking — not just a statement that marking exists — and that evidence must survive the kind of continuous measurement that the Council of AI operates. The Council of AI framework maps Art 50(2) onto the verified measurement credential: each synthetic-output batch can carry a signed provenance record (measure-point, board-manifest hash, model identifier, marking-method) that a third party can verify independently of the deployer's internal tools. This is the distinction between a marking that exists and a marking that is auditable. A vendor that applies a hidden watermark but refuses to publish the measurement protocol is not delivering Art 50(2) — the marking must be detectable by external instruments, not only by the deployer's own parser. The Council of AI measurement board (14 axes, frozen Ed25519 manifests) provides the external instrument: observations of marking-presence, marking-robustness under adversarial input, and marking-consistency across batches are recorded, signed, and made available for audit. The language must also be precise: the Council of AI does not claim that a marked output is 'safe' or 'isolated' — only that the marking has been continuously measured against a canonical reference and that the record of those measurements is signed and reproducible. That is monitored containment applied to the marking obligation. The regulation's effectiveness depends on whether third parties can verify the marking independently; a verification framework that requires trust in the deployer's platform fails the Article's intent. The Council of AI framework is designed specifically to close that gap.
